deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page is a working draft of the end of §19 and of §20 of Riemann's Inaugural Dissertation (Göttingen 1851), 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse'. The previous page drafts the beginning of the mapping theorem (§21 in print). The 'Lehrsatz des vorigen Art.' is the Dirichlet-principle theorem (§18 in print). It says: if a complex function α+βi is given on a surface T, and the functional Ω = ∫_T [(α_x − β_y)^2 + (α_y + β_x)^2] dT is finite, then α can be corrected by a function λ vanishing on the boundary. The result α+λ is the real part u of an analytic function u+iv of z. That function is unique, with the imaginary part fixed up to an additive constant.

(1) Lines 1-2. A line along which the boundary values jump can be treated as a cut (Schnitt) of the surface rather than as boundary. The arbitrariness of the data is then subject to certain restrictions.

(2) Admitting poles. Suppose that at a single point z0 a discontinuity of the type 'becoming infinite' is allowed. Then in the neighbourhood of z0 the function may be required to behave like an arbitrarily given function of z, namely a principal part P(z) = Σ_{k=1}^n c_k (z−z0)^{-k}. With the other conditions (boundary values of the real part, etc.) kept, the function is then completely determined.

Proof sketch, step by step:
- Choose the trial function a+bi (= α+βi) equal to P(z) inside an arbitrarily small circle K around z0.
- Outside K, choose it according to the previous conditions, joined continuously across ∂K.
- Inside K the trial function is analytic, so it satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations. The integrand of Ω (written on the page in abbreviated form as '∫ ∂α/∂x') therefore vanishes identically in K, and the integral over K is 0.
- Over the rest of T the integral equals a finite quantity, so Ω < ∞.
- Hence the Lehrsatz applies and gives an analytic function differing from α+βi by a function regular at z0. That function has the prescribed principal part at z0.
- Uniqueness: the difference of two solutions is regular everywhere, its real part vanishes on the boundary, so it is zero (up to an imaginary constant).

(3) Counting constants (generalisation). If the function may become infinite of order n at a point, 2n (real) constants become arbitrary. These are the real and imaginary parts of c_1,…,c_n [this reading of the count is my explanation]. Over several points the counts add.

(4) Geometric interpretation. A function continuous (analytic) in a given domain is represented as a mapping of the given plane surface onto another surface. The mapping keeps the connectivity and the form of the smallest parts, i.e. it is conformal.

(5) Boundary data as geometric conditions. The data determining the function refer either to boundary values or to discontinuities. They therefore all act as conditions on the position of the boundary of the image surface S. Either each data item gives a geometric locus for a single boundary point of S, or the data impose relations among points such that, once some are fixed, the others follow.

(6) Programme for analysis. The important functions for applications are those subject not to arbitrary data but to finitely many conditions. Example: the domain of z covers the whole infinite plane A once or several times (a closed Riemann surface). Then w must also be determined, as a function of 1/z, in a full neighbourhood of 1/z = 0. Inside the domain w may become infinite at isolated points of finite order. This leads in the printed text to rational and algebraic functions.
errors: No computational errors on the page. The steps are heuristic in the way all of Riemann's 1851 existence arguments are.
The Lehrsatz rests on the Dirichlet principle: existence of a minimiser of Ω is assumed, not proved (Weierstrass's critique of 1870; justified later by Hilbert 1900).
Joining the principal part continuously to the outer trial function needs the outer data to be adjustable near ∂K. This is easy but unstated.

The '2n constants' count tacitly takes the principal part as the free data with the boundary conditions held fixed. On a closed surface (point 6) the count must be corrected, which leads to Riemann–Roch type relations; that is not addressed here.

results.what: Existence and uniqueness of an analytic function with prescribed boundary real part and a prescribed pole/principal part, by subtracting the principal part and applying the Dirichlet principle
results.modern_name: Dirichlet principle with prescribed singularities (solving a Dirichlet problem with given principal parts)

results.what: A pole of order n contributes 2n arbitrary real constants
results.modern_name: Dimension count of principal parts (precursor of Riemann–Roch counting)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1851 (dissertation §19), developed in Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen 1857

results.what: Analytic function viewed as a conformal map preserving connectivity and the shape of infinitesimal parts
results.modern_name: Conformal mapping interpretation (prelude to the Riemann mapping theorem)

results.what: Functions on a domain covering the whole plane, regular at ∞ via 1/z, with finitely many finite-order poles
results.modern_name: Meromorphic functions on compact Riemann surfaces (rational/algebraic functions)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of known printed text: §§19–20 of Riemann's 1851 dissertation (poles allowed, 2n constants, conformal-map interpretation, functions over the whole plane). The content is fully published and attributed to him. Only minor drafting variants are of interest.

checkable.asserts: The integrand of Ω vanishes identically for a principal-part term (here z^-3), so the integral over the small circle K is 0. Expected result: 0.

checkable.sympy: x,y=symbols('x y',real=True); c1,c2,d1,d2=symbols('c1 c2 d1 d2',real=True); z=x+I*y; f=(c1+I*d1)/z+(c2+I*d2)/z**2; a=re(expand_complex(f)); b=im(expand_complex(f)); simplify(diff(a,x)-diff(b,y))
checkable.asserts: A general principal part of order 2 (4 = 2n real constants) satisfies Cauchy–Riemann. Expected result: 0.
A pole of order n=2 has n complex coefficients, i.e. 2n = 4 real constants.

transcription_corrections: The integral written as '∫ ∂α/∂x … über diesen Kreis erstreckt = 0' is Riemann's abbreviation of the Dirichlet integral Ω = ∫((∂α/∂x−∂β/∂y)^2+(∂α/∂y+∂β/∂x)^2)dT of the preceding article, not literally ∫∂α/∂x.
'a+bi' is the trial function (called α+βi on the previous page), not constants a, b.
'Lehrsatz des vorigen Art.' = the Dirichlet-principle theorem of the preceding article (§18 in the printed dissertation).
'Geometrisch dargestellt' (the interlinear correction) replaces 'stellt sich', in line with the printed §20 wording.
'Lage der Begrenzung von S' should probably be read with S as the image surface (Ξ on the previous page) rather than the original domain.
Several readings marked [?] are uncertain ('Ueberleitung', 'Schranke', 'erhält'). The page is heavily corrected, so the sense should be checked against printed §§19–20.
